Arkansas Tech University Unmanned
PEP 2025 White Paper
Team Members:
Isaac Broadway - isaacbroadway85@gmail.com
Charles Davis - charles13.davis@gmail.com
Treys Smedley - TreysSmedley3@gmail.com
Ethan Wooldrige - ethanbw172003@gmail.com
Lyndon Youngblood - lyoungblood03@gmail.com

Dr. Mohammad Amjadi - mamjadi@atu.edu

Background
This paper explores the development of an electric-powered, remote-controlled,
unmanned watercraft built to compete in a two-mile open ocean race. The design centers around
the innovative use of an existing stand-up jet ski hull and jet pump system, repurposed to support
electric propulsion and efficient motor cooling. The jet ski hull, originally engineered for high
speed and maneuverability, provides a robust structural foundation capable of accommodating
heavier components such as batteries and the electric motor. Choosing a larger hull—unlike any
used in previous years—offers greater stability in open ocean conditions and the potential for
increased speed.
A key innovation lies in the adaptation of the original jet pump, which was initially used
to propel the watercraft and cool a gas-powered engine. In our design, the jet pump's water
circulation system has been repurposed to cool the electric motor. Copper coils were wrapped
around the motor, allowing cool water to flow through and draw heat away during operation.
This ensures the motor remains at a safe operating temperature, even under high loads. This
approach not only simplifies the cooling system but also reduces overall weight and system
complexity. By utilizing pre-existing jet ski components, the design remains efficient, reliable,
and easier to maintain. The integration of the propulsion and cooling systems into a single,
cohesive unit marks a significant improvement over traditional electric watercraft designs.
Together, these features—using a large, stable hull and a repurposed jet pump for motor
cooling—form the foundation of an innovative and competitive ocean racing platform.
Design & Analysis
Hull Stability & Efficiency
Hull design played a pivotal role in the success of our electric-powered,
remote-controlled watercraft. After reviewing feedback from previous competitions, our team
identified hull stability as a critical factor—particularly in open-ocean conditions. Many teams
reported that their smaller crafts struggled to withstand large waves, with some capsizing
mid-race. With this in mind, we prioritized a larger, more stable platform capable of handling
unpredictable water conditions while supporting the weight of a high-power motor and a2

60-pound payload. We selected a stand-up jet ski hull due to its proven performance in
high-speed marine environments. Jet skis are designed to carry the weight of a full-grown rider,
maintain balance in rough water, and cut efficiently through waves. The hull’s size gave us
ample space for component layout and weight distribution, offering a perfect balance between
size, stability, and performance. The hull’s V-shaped design features a pointed bow that tapers
into a flatter rear section. This geometry provides several performance advantages across various
speeds. At low speeds, the wider rear creates greater surface area and buoyancy, enhancing
side-to-side stability and reducing the chance of tipping—especially during idle or tight turns. As
the craft accelerates, the hull transitions into planing mode, shifting more of the weight to the
rear. This reduces drag and allows the watercraft to ride on top of the water, resulting in a
smoother and more efficient ride. The sharp V-shaped bow also acts as a cutting edge, slicing
through waves and reducing hydrodynamic resistance, which contributes to greater speed and
improved handling in choppy conditions.
Despite the inherent stability of the jet ski hull, initial testing revealed a tendency for the
craft to roll side to side more than expected. This was largely due to the elevated center of
gravity caused by the placement of batteries and other heavy components. To address this issue,
we installed outriggers to widen the craft’s base. These significantly improved roll stability,
particularly at low speeds or while stationary. Although this modification increased drag and
slightly reduced our top-end speed, the trade-off in improved safety and control was well worth
it.
Beyond stability, the hull’s overall shape and construction were critical for efficiency.
The curvature—or deadrise—of the hull is optimized to minimize the wetted surface area,
reducing drag force as the watercraft moves forward. Jet skis typically use a deep-V or
modified-V design, which generates lift and allows the vessel to skim across the water surface
rather than plow through it. This reduces energy consumption and improves speed. The
integration of the jet pump into the hull further enhances hydrodynamic performance. The jet
pump draws water from directly beneath the hull, where pressure is highest, and propels it
through a nozzle to generate thrust. This efficient propulsion method minimizes turbulence and
contributes to smoother acceleration. Additionally, the hull’s smooth, sanded, and repainted
surface reduces friction with the water, further boosting efficiency and top-end speed.3

In summary, the jet ski hull served as a critical foundation for our design—offering the
perfect combination of stability, structural support, and hydrodynamic efficiency. From cutting
through waves with a sharp bow to gliding across the surface at speed, the hull's design
supported our mission to build a high-performing, ocean-capable electric watercraft.
Radio Frequency Control System
In order to achieve remote operation, we had to carefully choose our electrical
components for compatibility. The block diagram in Figure 1 explains the control system.
Figure 1: Radio Frequency Block Diagram.
The transmitter we chose was a Taranis X9D, which operates on the 2.4 GHz band and
has a transmission range of approximately 2.5 kilometers. The movement of the joysticks on the
transmitter sends radio signals to the receiver. We selected the Archer Plus R8 receiver, which is
fully compatible with the transmitter and outputs smooth Pulse Width Modulation (PWM)
signals. A PWM signal is a digital voltage signal that rapidly switches between high and low
states. Although it is not truly analog, varying the proportion of time the signal stays high within
each cycle—known as the duty cycle—can be used to simulate an analog voltage. For example, a
50% duty cycle means the signal is high for half of each cycle and low for the other half,
resulting in an average voltage that is approximately 50% of the maximum, shown below in
Figure 2. Since our system operates with a digital voltage range of 0–5V, a 50% duty cycle
yields an average voltage of around 2.5V.
Figure 2: Duty cycle visualization.4

The microcontroller we chose was an Arduino Uno R4, which is capable of both reading PWM
input signals and generating PWM outputs. The microcontroller receives power from a 12V
battery. Using C++ code, we mapped the PWM outputs from the receiver and generated new
PWM signals for motor control.
Primary Power Calculations
To determine the appropriate motor and battery configuration for our boat, we first
calculated the required horsepower to achieve our target speed of 15 miles per hour, which would
allow us to finish the race in approximately 8 minutes. This involved using power Equation 1.

In the equation, P is our electrical power, Fdis our drag force, and v is our target velocity. In
order to calculate our drag force acting on the hull, we used the standard drag Equation 2.

Where p is the density of water, Cdis the drag coefficient of our hull, A is the frontal area of the
hull contributing to drag, and v is the target velocity. After researching similarly sized hulls, we
estimated our drag coefficient to be 0.15 and our frontal area contributing to drag to be 0.35. This
yields a drag force of 1178 N. Going back to the power equation, this means we would need 7.9

Based on this, we selected two 48V, 30Ah lithium phosphate batteries wired in parallel,
providing a total capacity of 48V, 60Ah. We chose lithium phosphate batteries because they are
lighter than other chemistries. The selected batteries support a continuous discharge rate of 2.67C
(about 80A). Substituting into Ohm’s law yields a maximum power output of:
𝑃 = 𝐼𝑉 = 80𝐴 × 48𝑉 = 3. 84 𝑘𝑊 𝑝𝑒𝑟 𝑏𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑦
With both batteries, this puts us close to our 7.9 kW requirement and gives us about 20 minutes
of runtime, providing a solid margin above our 8-minute race duration while maintaining
efficiency and avoiding battery over-discharge.
Thermal Management
One of the key lessons we learned from last year’s competition was the importance of
thermal management. Several teams experienced motor overheating, which led to component
failure and ultimately prevented them from finishing the race. With this in mind, we made5

reliable motor cooling a top priority in our design. During early design discussions, our team
recognized that a jet ski offered a unique advantage—its built-in cooling system. In traditional
gas-powered jet skis, the jet pump is used not only for propulsion but also to circulate cool water
through the internal combustion engine to regulate temperature. We realized this existing system
could be adapted for our electric motor.
The jet pump works by using the impeller to force water through the intake and into the
hull. As high-pressure water exits through the nozzle, it creates a natural vacuum that pulls more
water through the system. We used this continuous flow to our advantage by routing the water
through ¼” copper tubing coiled tightly around the electric motor. As the cool water flows
through the copper coils, it absorbs the heat generated by the motor during operation. This heat
exchange process effectively pulls thermal energy away from the motor, maintaining a safe
operating temperature even under high loads. The use of copper tubing was
intentional—copper’s excellent thermal conductivity makes it ideal for transferring heat quickly
and efficiently. This passive cooling method is simple, reliable, and efficient. By repurposing the
jet ski’s original plumbing and cooling functionality, we were able to create an integrated thermal
management system without adding unnecessary weight or mechanical complexity. As a result,
our electric motor stays cooler, performs more efficiently, and is far less likely to overheat during
the demanding two-mile ocean race.
Heat Transfer Calculation
To understand and validate the effectiveness of our design, we analyzed the three stages
of heat transfer occurring between the motor and the water:
1. Conductive heat transfer from the stator to the aluminum housing
2. Conductive heat transfer from the aluminum housing to the copper tubing
3. Convective heat transfer from the copper tubing to the turbulent water flow
Based on Fourier’s Law, the temperature of the motor can be calculated by Equation 3
T1 = 𝒒 * RTotal + T2 (3)
Where:6

𝒒 = heat generated by the motor
RTotal = total thermal resistance of the system
T2 = ambient water temperature
Our motor ran at 51V and 120A, producing 6.12 kW of electrical power. We knew that our motor
would not operate at 100% efficiency, so after discussing efficiency ratings with the motor
manufacturer, we confirmed that our motor operates at approximately 85% efficiency. Using this
85% efficiency, we found that the motor produced 5.2 kW of mechanical power. The difference
between the two powers:
𝒒 = 6.12 kW−5.2 kW = 918 W (4)
This represents the heat that is generated during the operation of our motor. The T2 value could
be approximated using previous years' water temperature data at Virginia Beach. The
surrounding ocean water during the competition is estimated to be 62°F (289.82 K).
The first step is finding the thermal resistance (R-Value) of our motor’s aluminum
housing, RAlum. Thermal resistance can be calculated using the following equation:
RAlum = 𝐿/(𝑘 * 𝐴) (5)
Where:
L = material thickness
k = thermal conductivity
A= contact area
Now finding these values leads to a housing thickness of 5 mm, a thermal conductivity of 237
W/m·K for aluminum, and contact area of 0.095 m2. Plugging in these values results in a
R-Value of RAlum = 2.23*10-4 m²·K/W The next level of heat transfer can be solved in a similar
fashion using Equation 5 but this time solving for the R-Value between the aluminum and copper
tubing, RA2C. Given that we using ¼” copper tubing, the thickness is 1.245 mm, the thermal
conductivity is 401 W/m·K, and the contact area is 0.0635 m2. These values result in a R-Value
of RA2C = 7.743*10-5 m²·K/W. The last level of heat transfer between the copper tubing and the7

fresh flowing water is a little easier since the R-Value can be easily calculated. The overall heat
transfer coefficient, U, is a known value which is 450 W/m2·K. The R-Value can be found now
since the R-Value is equal to the inverse of U. The result is RC2W = 0.0022 m²·K/W.
Finally, the total R-Value can be found by summing all R-Values which results in Rtotal = 0.00252
m²·K/W. Using this new found Rtotal in Fourier's Law equation along with our calculated heat
generation and predicted water temperature will result in a temperature of our motor. Our
thermal model predicted a motor surface temperature of 66°F, which closely matched the
experimental data collected during an hour-long test under continuous load. This confirms the
effectiveness of our passive cooling system and validates our design approach.
Build Overview & Fabrication
Disassembly and Inspection
Once our team committed to the jet ski-based design for the electric-powered,
remote-controlled watercraft, we began searching for a suitable hull. After exploring various
options, we were fortunate to connect with a friend of a team member's father, who offered us an
old, “well-used” jet ski in exchange for repairing another one he owned. We quickly accepted the
offer and acquired the ski to begin the build process shown below in Figure 3.
Figure 3: Jet Ski Acquired.
Upon receiving the jet ski, we completely disassembled it, removing all components that
were damaged, outdated, or unnecessary for our electric design. The craft had been sitting in a
field for several years, and the interior cavity was filled with standing water, resulting in
significant corrosion to most of the internal components. After stripping the hull bare, we
conducted a full damage assessment. Fortunately, the structural integrity of the ski was largely8

intact, although we identified a large crack on the upper hull and several smaller cracks in the
hood. We began repairs by sanding all cracked areas and drilling relief holes at the ends of each
crack to prevent further spreading. Multiple layers of long-strand fiberglass were then applied to
reinforce these sections. Once cured, the fiberglass was sanded smooth to blend seamlessly with
the original hull, rendering the repairs nearly invisible. We followed this with a full cleaning of
the jet ski—removing decals, and rubber linings, and sanding down the entire surface in
preparation for repainting. To ensure durability, the hull was coated with six layers of
high-strength, scratch-resistant paint commonly used on tractor trailers.
Motor and Power Storage
With the hull structure restored, we took precise measurements of the internal cavity and
stand-up area to plan the placement of major components. These dimensions helped guide our
selection of the largest possible motor and battery configuration that could fit within the
constraints of the hull. After evaluating several power options and performing calculations based
on weight, voltage, and power demands, we determined that a 48V, 8-horsepower brushed DC
motor—capable of peaking at 15 horsepower—would be ideal for our application. To support
this motor, we selected two 48V batteries that could deliver the necessary current and fit within
the stand-up section of the hull. Once we secured funding for the competition, we ordered all
major components, including the motor, batteries, repair tooling, and various hardware items.
Steering and Motor Input
To steer the jet ski, we repurposed the existing steering cable that was originally
connected to the handlebars. Since the jet ski needed to be unmanned, we designed a system to
control steering a remote input. This system uses a linear actuator, Figure 4, mounted inside the
hull, which connects directly to the steering cable. A motor driver, which is powered by the same
12V battery that powers the Arduino, receives PWM input signals from the control system, and
with custom motor control logic written in C++, we direct the actuator's movement. When the
actuator extends, it pulls the steering cable in one direction, turning the nozzle—and the jet
ski—left. When it retracts, the nozzle turns right. The primary motor is controlled using similar
logic to the steering actuator. A separate, higher-powered motor driver receives PWM input
signals from the control system. Using motor control logic written in C++, we adjust the motor's9

speed based on these inputs. Due to the impeller-based propulsion system of the jet ski, there is
no capability for reverse thrust.
Figure 4: Linear Actuator.
Mechanical Fabrication and Repair
During a mechanical inspection, we discovered that the driveshaft was producing a
grinding noise. Disassembly of the carrier and jet pump revealed that the seals had become
brittle, and the bearings were severely corroded. We researched and ordered parts to totally repair
both components. The impeller was also scratched and chipped, so we hand-sanded and polished
it to improve efficiency. The rebuilt jet pump and carrier were reassembled and installed, with
impeller clearance adjusted to five-thousandths of an inch for optimal performance. The original
coupler was heavily corroded, with jagged teeth that risked damaging the motor shaft. We
replaced it with a CNC machined aluminum coupler for improved durability and precision. The
driveshaft, which was covered in rust, was also sanded and polished to a mirror-like finish to
ensure smooth operation and proper mating surface for seals.
Once we received the motor, we began designing the motor mount. We quickly realized
that our original concept wouldn't work due to a clearance issue. We pivoted to a vertical leg
mount design that would support the motor from the top rather than the bottom. Since our motor
is designed for vertical mounting, we fabricated a flat mounting plate from 1/4" thick steel,
repurposed from a SmartBoard stand. To maximize clearance at the bottom of the ski, the plate
was shaped with a fillet radius to match the motor's base. Our motor has 3.2 mm extrusions
around the mounting holes, so we face-milled a recessed dish in the plate to match the diameter
of the motor's mounting face. This allowed the plate to sit completely flush against the motor and10

ensured a solid, play-free connection. After cutting the four legs, we mocked everything
up—only to discover the legs didn’t fit correctly.
After reevaluating the setup, we spoke with one of our team member’s bosses, who
recommended scanning the interior of the hull to precisely measure each motor mount location
relative to the driveshaft centerline. Using a 3D scanner and PolyWorks, shown in Figure 5 (a),
we discovered that the motor mounts were not symmetrical—they were offset by 5/16" in the
front and 1/16" in the back. This meant each leg had to be custom-cut to fit its exact position.
With that data, we fabricated specific legs for each corner, then tacked and welded them to the
motor cage shown in Figure 5 (b).
Figure 5: (a) CAD model of Jetski interior (b) Welded Motor mount
Following final welding, we reinstalled the motor—only to find that the coupler spacing
was now slightly off, likely due to minor warping from welding. We determined that the motor
needed to be shimmed up by 1.17 mm to correct the alignment. Without access to precision
shims, we improvised with one of the most reliable materials available to college students: Red
Bull cans. We cut 1" x 1.5" aluminum squares from the cans and shimmed the legs until the
couplers had only 0.04 mm of side-to-side deviation. This final alignment ensured that the motor
was properly centered, allowing it to deliver maximum power to the driveshaft with minimal
vibration. The result was a solid, custom motor mounting system built from scratch with
creativity, precision, and a little caffeine.
Cooling System
To install the cooling system on our jet ski, we began by rebuilding the jet pump with
high-quality Nachi bearings and new seals to ensure optimal performance. The pump's interior11

was sanded and polished for smoother water flow. It featured two 1/4" brass ports—an inlet near
the impeller and an outlet at the rear—connected to the jet ski’s original hard-lined tubing using
flexible fuel lines. Since our electric motor would be cooled by copper coils, we needed at least
¼” of clearance between the motor and the hull. Before receiving funding for the motor, we
created a cardboard scale model to test fitment. This revealed clearance issues, so we notched out
the battery retainer and carefully sanded the cavity floor to gain the necessary space. To form the
cooling coil, we wrapped ¼” copper tubing around a slightly smaller diameter pipe so it would
coil tightly around the motor. We then installed the coils on to the motor with heat sink paste to
maximize heat transfer. With the jet pump rebuilt and the coils installed, we plumbed the system
to complete a functional open-loop water cooling setup.
Electrical Fabrication and Installation
To ensure solid electrical connections and minimize clutter in the cavity, we fabricated
custom-length wires using 2 AWG marine-grade cable to handle the high current demands.
Creating these cables required flux, solder, and a blowtorch.
To monitor live current draw and battery capacity, we installed a shunt on the ground side
of the primary power system. We also built a custom mount for the primary motor driver, along
with a dedicated mount for the steering actuator. Additionally, a separate mounting plate was
designed to securely hold a high-current fuse and contactor. Figure 6 is a full wiring diagram.
Figure 6: Full Wiring Diagram12

Testing and Refining
After completing our initial setup of our craft, we began testing to evaluate its
performance. Our testing was conducted in progressively more intense stages. This started with a
simple floating and balancing test, and worked up to a full 30 minutes of untethered driving.
During testing we quickly discovered a few issues, including several small holes creating
leakage, some excessive vibrations, and turning issues. To address the leaks, we sealed the holes
with silicone caulking as we found them through routine cavity checks during testing. When
trouble shooting the excessive vibrations we noticed that the coupler was misaligned by around 1
mm. We solved this problem by cutting out some metal shims out of aluminum cans and raising
the motor mount. This small adjustment tremendously reduced the vibration. Lastly, we
theorized that turning issues were stemming from improper mounting of the steering cable. After
remounting the cable, the steering issue was solved as well.
Risk
High-performance watercraft are subject to a wide range of risks, including water
leakage, overheating of critical components, electrical failure, and instability during operation.
This section provides a detailed account of the risks addressed during the design and build
stages, as well as the risks that will be actively controlled during the race.
Water Leakage
One of the main risks to address in the design is water intrusion. If water enters the hull,
it can damage critical components—such as the electrical systems and motor—potentially
leading to malfunctions, electrical shorts, or total system failure. To prevent this, several
strategies were implemented during the design and build phase. Generous amounts of silicone
sealant were applied to seams, joints, and other vulnerable areas to ensure a watertight structure.
In spots requiring additional reinforcement, “Flex Tape” glue was used to create extra layers of
protection. Custom 3D-printed components were also installed to cover pre-existing openings in
the hull, such as those for the gas cap, handlebars, and exhaust. These parts provide a lightweight
yet reliable way to maintain structural integrity. To further enhance water resistance, weather13

stripping was added between the hood and cavity, creating a secure seal when the hood is
latched.
Cooling Systems
Overheating is another risk that can have a serious impact on performance, especially
within our motor and battery design. To keep temperatures in check, copper coils are wrapped
around the motor to help dissipate heat through heat transfer. Cold water from the jet pump is
pumped through these coils to keep the motor cool during operation as shown in Figure 7 (a),
even under high stress. The jet pump plays a crucial role by circulating the water through the
coils, ensuring the motor doesn’t overheat, which would lead to a decline in performance or
permanent damage.
Electrical Concerns
The battery, which powers the primary drive system, was tested to ensure it can last
through the full 2-mile race without overheating or depleting prematurely. We installed a shunt
through the primary motor wiring that allows us to monitor the current draw via an onboard
display as shown in Figure 7 (b). With the current data, we can determine safe temperature
levels.
Figure 7: (a) Motor Cooling System (b) Battery Monitoring Display
Electrical efficiency is a critical factor in ensuring the smooth operation of the watercraft.
The system must handle high current loads without overheating, so 2 AWG wiring was selected
to minimize heat buildup and maintain safe operating temperatures. To protect against current14

surges, fuses and contactors were installed—these safety components will either blow or
disconnect the circuit if current levels exceed safe thresholds. Our batteries also have a built in
battery management system (BMS) that helps discharge current at a healthy rate without
overworking our batteries and causing malfunctions. Component compatibility was also a key
consideration during the design phase. Every element of the electrical system—from the fuse and
contactor to the driver and motor—was carefully chosen to ensure seamless integration and
reliable performance.
Hull Stability
Stability is a critical concern for the watercraft, especially at high speeds. Weight
distribution was carefully evaluated, and a preliminary weight test was conducted to determine
the optimal placement for the batteries and other payloads. Initial testing revealed insufficient
lateral stability, prompting the installation of outriggers (Figure 8 (b)). These outriggers
significantly enhance the vessel’s balance, helping it stay upright and stable during sharp turns
and sudden maneuvers. Also, in the event of a capsize, the battery box was designed to remain
secure during rapid acceleration and wave impacts. All electrical connections inside the box are
insulated with rubber caps and firmly fastened to reduce the risk of short-circuiting or other
failures caused by water exposure. To enhance safety—and in compliance with competition
regulations—an emergency stop button was integrated into the battery box, allowing the circuit
to be manually shut off in a worst-case scenario (Figure 8 (b)). The box itself is constructed from
high-strength plastic and sealed with waterproof gaskets to ensure durability and protect the
batteries in harsh conditions.
Figure 8: a) Adjustable Outriggers, b) Battery box design featuring E-Stop Button15

Finally, the watercraft had to be structurally reinforced to support the motor, withstand the
weight of the batteries and payload, and endure the stress of waves. When we first acquired the
watercraft, there was a large crack in the hull and several smaller cracks in the hood. These
issues needed to be addressed to ensure the structural integrity of the craft during extended use.
To repair the damage, multiple layers of long-strand fiberglass were applied, then sanded smooth
and repainted to restore the original finish seamlessly.
Once the watercraft is in operation, there are still several risks that need to be carefully
monitored and controlled in real time, especially during a race. Signal strength is one of these
risks. Losing communication between the watercraft and the controller can lead to operational
failures. To ensure strong, reliable communication, a long-range transmitter and receiver were
acquired so that the craft could reach distances of almost a mile.

In summary, the jet ski hull served as a critical foundation for our design—offering the
perfect combination of stability, structural support, and hydrodynamic efficiency. From cutting
through waves with a sharp bow to gliding across the surface at speed, the hull's design
supported our mission to build a high-performing, ocean-capable electric watercraft.
Radio Frequency Control System
In order to achieve remote operation, we had to carefully choose our electrical
components for compatibility. The block diagram in Figure 1 explains the control system.
Figure 1: Radio Frequency Block Diagram.
The transmitter we chose was a Taranis X9D, which operates on the 2.4 GHz band and
has a transmission range of approximately 2.5 kilometers. The movement of the joysticks on the
transmitter sends radio signals to the receiver. We selected the Archer Plus R8 receiver, which is
fully compatible with the transmitter and outputs smooth Pulse Width Modulation (PWM)
signals. A PWM signal is a digital voltage signal that rapidly switches between high and low
states. Although it is not truly analog, varying the proportion of time the signal stays high within
each cycle—known as the duty cycle—can be used to simulate an analog voltage. For example, a
50% duty cycle means the signal is high for half of each cycle and low for the other half,
resulting in an average voltage that is approximately 50% of the maximum, shown below in
Figure 2. Since our system operates with a digital voltage range of 0–5V, a 50% duty cycle
yields an average voltage of around 2.5V.
Figure 2: Duty cycle visualization.4
The microcontroller we chose was an Arduino Uno R4, which is capable of both reading PWM
input signals and generating PWM outputs. The microcontroller receives power from a 12V
battery. Using C++ code, we mapped the PWM outputs from the receiver and generated new
PWM signals for motor control.

Thermal Management
One of the key lessons we learned from last year’s competition was the importance of
thermal management. Several teams experienced motor overheating, which led to component
failure and ultimately prevented them from finishing the race. With this in mind, we made5
reliable motor cooling a top priority in our design. During early design discussions, our team
recognized that a jet ski offered a unique advantage—its built-in cooling system. In traditional
gas-powered jet skis, the jet pump is used not only for propulsion but also to circulate cool water
through the internal combustion engine to regulate temperature. We realized this existing system
could be adapted for our electric motor.
The jet pump works by using the impeller to force water through the intake and into the
hull. As high-pressure water exits through the nozzle, it creates a natural vacuum that pulls more
water through the system. We used this continuous flow to our advantage by routing the water
through ¼” copper tubing coiled tightly around the electric motor. As the cool water flows
through the copper coils, it absorbs the heat generated by the motor during operation. This heat
exchange process effectively pulls thermal energy away from the motor, maintaining a safe
operating temperature even under high loads. The use of copper tubing was
intentional—copper’s excellent thermal conductivity makes it ideal for transferring heat quickly
and efficiently. This passive cooling method is simple, reliable, and efficient. By repurposing the
jet ski’s original plumbing and cooling functionality, we were able to create an integrated thermal
management system without adding unnecessary weight or mechanical complexity. As a result,
our electric motor stays cooler, performs more efficiently, and is far less likely to overheat during
the demanding two-mile ocean race.

To understand and validate the effectiveness of our design, we analyzed the three stages
of heat transfer occurring between the motor and the water:
1. Conductive heat transfer from the stator to the aluminum housing
2. Conductive heat transfer from the aluminum housing to the copper tubing
3. Convective heat transfer from the copper tubing to the turbulent water flow

Build Overview & Fabrication
Disassembly and Inspection
Once our team committed to the jet ski-based design for the electric-powered,
remote-controlled watercraft, we began searching for a suitable hull. After exploring various
options, we were fortunate to connect with a friend of a team member's father, who offered us an
old, “well-used” jet ski in exchange for repairing another one he owned. We quickly accepted the
offer and acquired the ski to begin the build process shown below in Figure 3.
Figure 3: Jet Ski Acquired.
Upon receiving the jet ski, we completely disassembled it, removing all components that
were damaged, outdated, or unnecessary for our electric design. The craft had been sitting in a
field for several years, and the interior cavity was filled with standing water, resulting in
significant corrosion to most of the internal components. After stripping the hull bare, we
conducted a full damage assessment. Fortunately, the structural integrity of the ski was largely8
intact, although we identified a large crack on the upper hull and several smaller cracks in the
hood. We began repairs by sanding all cracked areas and drilling relief holes at the ends of each
crack to prevent further spreading. Multiple layers of long-strand fiberglass were then applied to
reinforce these sections. Once cured, the fiberglass was sanded smooth to blend seamlessly with
the original hull, rendering the repairs nearly invisible. We followed this with a full cleaning of
the jet ski—removing decals, and rubber linings, and sanding down the entire surface in
preparation for repainting. To ensure durability, the hull was coated with six layers of
high-strength, scratch-resistant paint commonly used on tractor trailers.
Motor and Power Storage
With the hull structure restored, we took precise measurements of the internal cavity and
stand-up area to plan the placement of major components. These dimensions helped guide our
selection of the largest possible motor and battery configuration that could fit within the
constraints of the hull. After evaluating several power options and performing calculations based
on weight, voltage, and power demands, we determined that a 48V, 8-horsepower brushed DC
motor—capable of peaking at 15 horsepower—would be ideal for our application. To support
this motor, we selected two 48V batteries that could deliver the necessary current and fit within
the stand-up section of the hull. Once we secured funding for the competition, we ordered all
major components, including the motor, batteries, repair tooling, and various hardware items.
Steering and Motor Input
To steer the jet ski, we repurposed the existing steering cable that was originally
connected to the handlebars. Since the jet ski needed to be unmanned, we designed a system to
control steering a remote input. This system uses a linear actuator, Figure 4, mounted inside the
hull, which connects directly to the steering cable. A motor driver, which is powered by the same
12V battery that powers the Arduino, receives PWM input signals from the control system, and
with custom motor control logic written in C++, we direct the actuator's movement. When the
actuator extends, it pulls the steering cable in one direction, turning the nozzle—and the jet
ski—left. When it retracts, the nozzle turns right. The primary motor is controlled using similar
logic to the steering actuator. A separate, higher-powered motor driver receives PWM input
signals from the control system. Using motor control logic written in C++, we adjust the motor's9
speed based on these inputs. Due to the impeller-based propulsion system of the jet ski, there is
no capability for reverse thrust.
Figure 4: Linear Actuator.
Mechanical Fabrication and Repair
During a mechanical inspection, we discovered that the driveshaft was producing a
grinding noise. Disassembly of the carrier and jet pump revealed that the seals had become
brittle, and the bearings were severely corroded. We researched and ordered parts to totally repair
both components. The impeller was also scratched and chipped, so we hand-sanded and polished
it to improve efficiency. The rebuilt jet pump and carrier were reassembled and installed, with
impeller clearance adjusted to five-thousandths of an inch for optimal performance. The original
coupler was heavily corroded, with jagged teeth that risked damaging the motor shaft. We
replaced it with a CNC machined aluminum coupler for improved durability and precision. The
driveshaft, which was covered in rust, was also sanded and polished to a mirror-like finish to
ensure smooth operation and proper mating surface for seals.
Once we received the motor, we began designing the motor mount. We quickly realized
that our original concept wouldn't work due to a clearance issue. We pivoted to a vertical leg
mount design that would support the motor from the top rather than the bottom. Since our motor
is designed for vertical mounting, we fabricated a flat mounting plate from 1/4" thick steel,
repurposed from a SmartBoard stand. To maximize clearance at the bottom of the ski, the plate
was shaped with a fillet radius to match the motor's base. Our motor has 3.2 mm extrusions
around the mounting holes, so we face-milled a recessed dish in the plate to match the diameter
of the motor's mounting face. This allowed the plate to sit completely flush against the motor and10
ensured a solid, play-free connection. After cutting the four legs, we mocked everything
up—only to discover the legs didn’t fit correctly.
After reevaluating the setup, we spoke with one of our team member’s bosses, who
recommended scanning the interior of the hull to precisely measure each motor mount location
relative to the driveshaft centerline. Using a 3D scanner and PolyWorks, shown in Figure 5 (a),
we discovered that the motor mounts were not symmetrical—they were offset by 5/16" in the
front and 1/16" in the back. This meant each leg had to be custom-cut to fit its exact position.
With that data, we fabricated specific legs for each corner, then tacked and welded them to the
motor cage shown in Figure 5 (b).
Figure 5: (a) CAD model of Jetski interior (b) Welded Motor mount
Following final welding, we reinstalled the motor—only to find that the coupler spacing
was now slightly off, likely due to minor warping from welding. We determined that the motor
needed to be shimmed up by 1.17 mm to correct the alignment. Without access to precision
shims, we improvised with one of the most reliable materials available to college students: Red
Bull cans. We cut 1" x 1.5" aluminum squares from the cans and shimmed the legs until the
couplers had only 0.04 mm of side-to-side deviation. This final alignment ensured that the motor
was properly centered, allowing it to deliver maximum power to the driveshaft with minimal
vibration. The result was a solid, custom motor mounting system built from scratch with
creativity, precision, and a little caffeine.
Cooling System
To install the cooling system on our jet ski, we began by rebuilding the jet pump with
high-quality Nachi bearings and new seals to ensure optimal performance. The pump's interior11
was sanded and polished for smoother water flow. It featured two 1/4" brass ports—an inlet near
the impeller and an outlet at the rear—connected to the jet ski’s original hard-lined tubing using
flexible fuel lines. Since our electric motor would be cooled by copper coils, we needed at least
¼” of clearance between the motor and the hull. Before receiving funding for the motor, we
created a cardboard scale model to test fitment. This revealed clearance issues, so we notched out
the battery retainer and carefully sanded the cavity floor to gain the necessary space. To form the
cooling coil, we wrapped ¼” copper tubing around a slightly smaller diameter pipe so it would
coil tightly around the motor. We then installed the coils on to the motor with heat sink paste to
maximize heat transfer. With the jet pump rebuilt and the coils installed, we plumbed the system
to complete a functional open-loop water cooling setup.
Electrical Fabrication and Installation
To ensure solid electrical connections and minimize clutter in the cavity, we fabricated
custom-length wires using 2 AWG marine-grade cable to handle the high current demands.
Creating these cables required flux, solder, and a blowtorch.
To monitor live current draw and battery capacity, we installed a shunt on the ground side
of the primary power system. We also built a custom mount for the primary motor driver, along
with a dedicated mount for the steering actuator. Additionally, a separate mounting plate was
designed to securely hold a high-current fuse and contactor. Figure 6 is a full wiring diagram.
Figure 6: Full Wiring Diagram12
Testing and Refining
After completing our initial setup of our craft, we began testing to evaluate its
performance. Our testing was conducted in progressively more intense stages. This started with a
simple floating and balancing test, and worked up to a full 30 minutes of untethered driving.
During testing we quickly discovered a few issues, including several small holes creating
leakage, some excessive vibrations, and turning issues. To address the leaks, we sealed the holes
with silicone caulking as we found them through routine cavity checks during testing. When
trouble shooting the excessive vibrations we noticed that the coupler was misaligned by around 1
mm. We solved this problem by cutting out some metal shims out of aluminum cans and raising
the motor mount. This small adjustment tremendously reduced the vibration. Lastly, we
theorized that turning issues were stemming from improper mounting of the steering cable. After
remounting the cable, the steering issue was solved as well.
Risk
High-performance watercraft are subject to a wide range of risks, including water
leakage, overheating of critical components, electrical failure, and instability during operation.
This section provides a detailed account of the risks addressed during the design and build
stages, as well as the risks that will be actively controlled during the race.
Water Leakage
One of the main risks to address in the design is water intrusion. If water enters the hull,
it can damage critical components—such as the electrical systems and motor—potentially
leading to malfunctions, electrical shorts, or total system failure. To prevent this, several
strategies were implemented during the design and build phase. Generous amounts of silicone
sealant were applied to seams, joints, and other vulnerable areas to ensure a watertight structure.
In spots requiring additional reinforcement, “Flex Tape” glue was used to create extra layers of
protection. Custom 3D-printed components were also installed to cover pre-existing openings in
the hull, such as those for the gas cap, handlebars, and exhaust. These parts provide a lightweight
yet reliable way to maintain structural integrity. To further enhance water resistance, weather13
stripping was added between the hood and cavity, creating a secure seal when the hood is
latched.
Cooling Systems
Overheating is another risk that can have a serious impact on performance, especially
within our motor and battery design. To keep temperatures in check, copper coils are wrapped
around the motor to help dissipate heat through heat transfer. Cold water from the jet pump is
pumped through these coils to keep the motor cool during operation as shown in Figure 7 (a),
even under high stress. The jet pump plays a crucial role by circulating the water through the
coils, ensuring the motor doesn’t overheat, which would lead to a decline in performance or
permanent damage.
Electrical Concerns
The battery, which powers the primary drive system, was tested to ensure it can last
through the full 2-mile race without overheating or depleting prematurely. We installed a shunt
through the primary motor wiring that allows us to monitor the current draw via an onboard
display as shown in Figure 7 (b). With the current data, we can determine safe temperature
levels.
Figure 7: (a) Motor Cooling System (b) Battery Monitoring Display
Electrical efficiency is a critical factor in ensuring the smooth operation of the watercraft.
The system must handle high current loads without overheating, so 2 AWG wiring was selected
to minimize heat buildup and maintain safe operating temperatures. To protect against current14
surges, fuses and contactors were installed—these safety components will either blow or
disconnect the circuit if current levels exceed safe thresholds. Our batteries also have a built in
battery management system (BMS) that helps discharge current at a healthy rate without
overworking our batteries and causing malfunctions. Component compatibility was also a key
consideration during the design phase. Every element of the electrical system—from the fuse and
contactor to the driver and motor—was carefully chosen to ensure seamless integration and
reliable performance.
Hull Stability
Stability is a critical concern for the watercraft, especially at high speeds. Weight
distribution was carefully evaluated, and a preliminary weight test was conducted to determine
the optimal placement for the batteries and other payloads. Initial testing revealed insufficient
lateral stability, prompting the installation of outriggers (Figure 8 (b)). These outriggers
significantly enhance the vessel’s balance, helping it stay upright and stable during sharp turns
and sudden maneuvers. Also, in the event of a capsize, the battery box was designed to remain
secure during rapid acceleration and wave impacts. All electrical connections inside the box are
insulated with rubber caps and firmly fastened to reduce the risk of short-circuiting or other
failures caused by water exposure. To enhance safety—and in compliance with competition
regulations—an emergency stop button was integrated into the battery box, allowing the circuit
to be manually shut off in a worst-case scenario (Figure 8 (b)). The box itself is constructed from
high-strength plastic and sealed with waterproof gaskets to ensure durability and protect the
batteries in harsh conditions.
Figure 8: a) Adjustable Outriggers, b) Battery box design featuring E-Stop Button15
Finally, the watercraft had to be structurally reinforced to support the motor, withstand the
weight of the batteries and payload, and endure the stress of waves. When we first acquired the
watercraft, there was a large crack in the hull and several smaller cracks in the hood. These
issues needed to be addressed to ensure the structural integrity of the craft during extended use.
To repair the damage, multiple layers of long-strand fiberglass were applied, then sanded smooth
and repainted to restore the original finish seamlessly.
Once the watercraft is in operation, there are still several risks that need to be carefully
monitored and controlled in real time, especially during a race. Signal strength is one of these
risks. Losing communication between the watercraft and the controller can lead to operational
failures. To ensure strong, reliable communication, a long-range transmitter and receiver were
acquired so that the craft could reach distances of almost a mile.
